neighbors.heading: these and these
neighbors.text: Today two cousins argued over a book, and an aunt brought tea. Jews tell of two old schools, Hillel's and Shammai's, who argued for years. The Talmud says a voice from heaven called both views the words of the living God, and the law followed Hillel because his school was kind and humble, and taught Shammai's view before its own.
neighbors.difference: The Talmud keeps both sides of the argument on the page, so later readers go on weighing them. The Sikh lesson keeps the shared daily prayers steady in the middle, so worship doesn't wait on the debate.
neighbors.shared: a good argument starts by listening, and ends with both still at the table.

neighbors.heading: know the other side
neighbors.text: Today two cousins argued, and an aunt said: sit down, and say it again, slowly. The philosopher John Stuart Mill made listening part of clear thinking: "He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that." To hold a view well, he said, hear the other side from people who truly believe it, at its strongest.
neighbors.difference: Mill argued for open debate so truth could come out in a free society, with no scripture at the center. In the Sikh lesson, listening is part of a life of faith, and the Guru's word is the shared ground.
neighbors.shared: you understand your own view better once you've really heard theirs.
neighbors.sources: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, chapter 2

neighbors.heading: better than sleep
neighbors.text: Today the house was dark, and someone washed and began to remember before the day began. Muslims know that hour too. Before dawn, the call to the Fajr prayer adds a line: prayer is better than sleep. Muslims wash first, the wudu, then pray. The Qur'an says of that hour: "Lo! (the recital of) the Qur'an at dawn is ever witnessed."
neighbors.difference: Fajr is one of the set daily prayers, with fixed words, standing, bowing and prostrating toward Mecca. The Sikh amrit vela is sitting with the Name, Waheguru, and the morning banis, with no set direction to face.
neighbors.shared: the first words of the day go to God, before anything else gets them.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 17:78 (Pickthall 1930) · the dawn call to prayer, as-salatu khayrun min an-nawm (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the hour before sunrise
neighbors.text: Today someone woke in the dark, bathed, and turned the mind to God first. Hindus have a name for that stretch of dark: brahma muhurta, the time before sunrise. The law book of Manu tells a householder to wake then and reflect. Hindu morning worship traditionally begins with a bath, and the Gayatri mantra is chanted as the sun comes up.
neighbors.difference: Hindu morning rites can include a lamp, offerings, or water poured to the rising sun. The Sikh hour has no offering or image: the bath readies the body, and remembering the Name is the whole of it.
neighbors.shared: the quiet before sunrise is a good place to remember.
neighbors.sources: Manusmriti 4.92 (paraphrase) · Rig Veda 3.62.10, the Gayatri mantra (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not by birth
neighbors.text: Today the Sikh code set caste down, with the charms and lucky days. The Buddha also met a world that ranked people by birth, and he turned the name of the highest caste into a name for goodness: "A man does not become a Brâhmana by his platted hair, by his family, or by birth; in whom there is truth and righteousness, he is blessed, he is a Brâhmana."
neighbors.difference: The Buddha kept the old word, brahmin, and gave it a new meaning: a person of virtue. The Sikh code sets caste names aside altogether, and roots equality in the one light shining in every person.
neighbors.shared: nobody's worth is written in the family they were born into.

neighbors.heading: neither bond nor free
neighbors.text: Today the code set caste down: who counts as higher, whose cup can't be shared. The first Christians had walls of their own, between peoples, between slave and free, between men and women. Paul wrote to the Galatians: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."
neighbors.difference: For Paul, the walls fall through faith and baptism into Christ. In Sikh teaching, they fall because the same light already shines in every person, which is why everyone eats in the same row at langar.
neighbors.shared: the table is long enough for everyone, and nobody sits higher.

neighbors.heading: say it out loud
neighbors.text: Today a Sikh who broke a promise walked to the front of the room instead of hiding. Recovery groups know that road. The fifth of the Twelve Steps of Alcoholics Anonymous asks a person to admit to God, to themselves, and to another human being the exact nature of their wrongs. Not to stay ashamed: to stop carrying a secret.
neighbors.difference: In the Twelve Steps, the admission is usually made privately to one trusted person, and no penalty is set. In the Sikh code, it's made before the gathered sangat, and five Sikhs set the penance.
neighbors.shared: a mistake said out loud loses some of its power over you.
neighbors.sources: Alcoholics Anonymous, the Twelve Steps, step five (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: confess one to another
neighbors.text: Today the way home went through the front of the room: say what you did, accept the penance, stand again. Catholics walk a road like it in confession. The letter of James says: "Confess therefore your sins one to another: and pray one for another, that you may be saved." The priest gives a penance, speaks the words of absolution, and sends the person out in peace.
neighbors.difference: Catholic confession is private, to a priest bound by the seal never to repeat it, and it's a sacrament in which Christ forgives. A tankhah is heard openly, by five Sikhs, in front of the sangat.
neighbors.shared: owning a wrong is the first step home, not the last word.
neighbors.sources: James 5:16 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1424, 1467 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: making it right
neighbors.text: Today a mistake was answered with work: a week at the shoe counter, the dishes, a set prayer each morning. Hindu law books call amends prayashchitta. Manu's code lists ways a wrongdoer is freed: owning the wrong, regret, self-discipline, reciting sacred verses, and, when nothing else is possible, giving. The mending is done, not only felt.
neighbors.difference: Prayashchitta is often set by learned priests and can include fasting, pilgrimage or ritual. A tankhah is set by five Sikhs from the sangat, and leans toward hands-on service or reciting bani.
neighbors.shared: a wrong is mended by what you do next, in the open.

neighbors.heading: go and make peace
neighbors.text: Today a penance looked like a volunteer shift by the front door. Jewish teaching joins repair to repentance too. The Mishnah says Yom Kippur atones for wrongs between a person and God, but a wrong against another person isn't atoned until you make peace with them. The High Holiday prayers name what softens a hard decree: repentance, prayer and tzedakah, giving.
neighbors.difference: In Jewish teaching, the repair is owed first to the person you hurt, and no panel needs to set it. In the Sikh code, five Sikhs set the tankhah, and the service often goes to the whole sangat.
neighbors.shared: sorry is a start; the mending happens with your hands.
neighbors.sources: Mishnah Yoma 8:9 (paraphrase) · Unetaneh Tokef, High Holiday liturgy (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: it seemed good to us
neighbors.text: Today the whole panth gathered before the Guru to decide hard things as one. The early church faced a hard question too: what to ask of newcomers who weren't Jewish. "And the apostles and elders came together for to consider of this matter." After long debate, their letter to the churches said: "For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us."
neighbors.difference: Many churches look back to that Jerusalem gathering as a pattern for later councils of bishops and elders. A gurmatta is made by the gathered Khalsa before the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs still debate who can call one today.
neighbors.shared: the hardest questions are best decided together, before God.

neighbors.heading: a matter of counsel
neighbors.text: Today the whole panth gathered in the Guru's presence to decide as one. The Qur'an praises believers "whose affairs are a matter of counsel": they decide together. The word is shura, consultation. The Qur'an even tells the Prophet himself to consult his companions on the conduct of affairs, and then, once resolved, to put his trust in God.
neighbors.difference: Shura is counsel: in Islamic tradition, leaders and communities weigh advice within the guidance of the Qur'an and the Prophet's example. A gurmatta is a resolution of the gathered Khalsa before the Guru Granth Sahib, meant to bind all.
neighbors.shared: nobody should decide everyone's future alone.

neighbors.heading: be filled instead
neighbors.text: Today a guest asked for lime soda, and the Gurus spoke of another drink: the Name. Paul writes something close: "And be not drunk with wine, wherein is luxury; but be ye filled with the holy Spirit." One fullness in place of another. The Church names the virtue temperance, which keeps pleasures in balance so the mind stays its own.
neighbors.difference: Catholics aren't asked to give up alcohol: wine is consecrated at every Mass, and drinking in moderation is fine. The Sikh code asks Sikhs to refuse alcohol, tobacco and intoxicants entirely.
neighbors.shared: a clear mind is kept for what matters most.
neighbors.sources: Ephesians 5:18 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1809, 2290 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the fifth precept
neighbors.text: Today a guest in a turban smiled and turned down the drink, to keep his mind clear. Buddhists make a promise like it. The fifth of the five precepts that lay Buddhists recite is to refrain from wine and liquor that cause heedlessness. Heedlessness is the word to notice: the Buddha's teaching asks a person to stay awake to what's happening now.
neighbors.difference: For Buddhists, the clear mind serves mindfulness and wisdom, with no creator God in view. For Sikhs, it's kept for remembering God, the Name, and for seeing God in other people.
neighbors.shared: staying clear-headed is a way of staying awake to life.
neighbors.sources: the five precepts, fifth precept (Pali, paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: statutes into songs
neighbors.text: Today the code's disciplines turned out to be the shape joy lives in, the way a raga holds a song. A psalm says it of God's law: "Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage." Another calls out: "Serve the LORD with gladness." And once a year, on Simchat Torah, Jews dance with the Torah scrolls in their arms.
neighbors.difference: In Judaism the joy centers on the commandments themselves, the mitzvot, as a gift to keep. In Sikh teaching, the joy comes from finding the Guru, and the code is the frame that holds it.
neighbors.shared: a discipline kept with love can feel more like music than rules.

neighbors.heading: glad to do it
neighbors.text: Today the code turned out to be like a raga: rules that make music instead of noise. Aristotle thought the same about good habits. At first a discipline is effort. Practiced long enough, he said, it becomes your character, and the sign is that you take pleasure in it: the generous person enjoys giving, and the brave one isn't miserable being brave.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle's joy grows from habits built by reason and practice, with no Guru or God needed. In the Sikh hymn, joy comes by finding the Guru, and the discipline gives it a home.
neighbors.shared: practice long enough, and the hard thing becomes a glad thing.
neighbors.sources: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapter 3 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: no reward nor thanks
neighbors.text: Today we met the Sevapanthis, heirs of Bhai Kanhaiya, who gave water to wounded men without asking whose side they were on. The Qur'an describes the righteous who "feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him," saying: "We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." Even the captive, the one from the other side, is fed.
neighbors.difference: In the Qur'an, the givers feed others for God's sake, in awe of a Day to come. The Sevapanthi story centers on seeing the Guru's face in every person, friend or enemy.
neighbors.shared: serve the one in front of you without asking whose side they're on.

neighbors.heading: the same in every one
neighbors.text: Today we met the Sevapanthis, who served travelers and the sick without asking who anyone was. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the wise look with the same eye on a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcaste. He also teaches action without grasping at its fruits: do the work, and let go of the reward.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, selfless action is often taught as doing one's own duty as an offering to God. Sevapanthi seva is chosen work for strangers, water, food and rest, wherever it's needed, with nothing asked back.
neighbors.shared: the work is the gift; nobody needs to applaud.

neighbors.heading: chanting through the night
neighbors.text: Today a hall sang the Guru's hymns from midnight to gray dawn. In Sri Lanka and other Theravada lands, monks chant paritta, protective verses from the Buddha's teaching, sometimes through a whole night. One is the Metta Sutta, which wishes: may all beings be happy. Families gather, a thread runs from the monks' hands around the room, and the words go on.
neighbors.difference: Kirtan is praise of God, with the whole sangat singing back. Paritta is the Buddha's teaching, led by monks for protection and blessing, and it addresses no creator God.
neighbors.shared: some words are worth staying awake all night to hear.
neighbors.sources: Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (paraphrase) · Theravada paritta chanting (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: at midnight, singing
neighbors.text: Today a hall sang until gray light came through the windows. Christians know night songs too. Locked in prison, "at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them." Luke says Jesus once "continued all night in prayer to God." Monks still rise in the dark to sing psalms, and churches keep a vigil the night before Easter.
neighbors.difference: Christian night prayer is often sung by a choir or a community of monks, and prayed to the Father through Christ. In akhand kirtan, the whole sangat sings the Guru's hymns back, line by line, in remembrance of the Name.
neighbors.shared: a song kept going through the dark can carry a whole room.

neighbors.heading: no, they are people
neighbors.text: Today the Guru handed everyone the same name, so no one's birth could be read off it. The Stoic Seneca pushed against the labels of his own Rome. People say: they are slaves. No, he answered, they are human beings, housemates, humble friends. The one you call a slave, he wrote, was born of the same seed and lives under the same sky.
neighbors.difference: Seneca urged respect inside a world he didn't overturn: slavery stayed, and he owned slaves. The Sikh shared name aims at the ranking itself, though Sikhs say honestly that caste names still linger.
neighbors.shared: a label is the least true thing about a person.

neighbors.heading: no respect of persons
neighbors.text: Today a shared name kept strangers from reading anyone's caste. The letter of James paints a church door: a man walks in with gold rings and fine clothes, another in shabby ones. Give the rich man the good seat and send the poor one to stand, James says, and you've made distinctions and judged badly. In baptism, every Catholic receives the same new life.
neighbors.difference: Catholics keep their family names; equality comes through one baptism into the one Body of Christ. Sikh teaching made the shared name itself, Singh and Kaur, the sign that birth sets no rank.
neighbors.shared: everyone who walks in deserves the good seat.
neighbors.sources: James 2:1-4 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1267 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: waking, and rest
neighbors.text: Today the Granth was carried at dawn to its high seat, and at night, in a palanquin, to rest. Some Hindu temples keep a day like it. Before dawn, priests sing the deity awake with a suprabhatam, a morning song. Through the day come baths, offerings and darshan, seeing and being seen. At night, the deity is laid down to rest.
neighbors.difference: In a Hindu temple, the image is honored as God present in form. Sikhs bow to no image: the Granth is the Guru as Word, cared for the way you'd care for a revered teacher living in your house.
neighbors.shared: what you love, you wake gently and lay down gently.
neighbors.sources: Venkatesa Suprabhatam (paraphrase) · Hindu temple daily worship (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: when the ark rested
neighbors.text: Today the Granth was carried at dawn to its seat and at night to rest. Jews carry their scripture too. On the Sabbath, the Torah scroll is taken from the ark and carried through the congregation, and people reach out to touch it with a prayer shawl or a prayer book. When it goes back, they sing the verse Moses spoke when the ark came to rest.
neighbors.difference: The Torah is honored as God's teaching, given at Sinai, not as a living person; between readings it rests in the ark. Sikhs treat the Granth as the living Guru, who wakes, speaks, and rests.
neighbors.shared: a holy book can be carried like someone deeply loved.
neighbors.sources: Numbers 10:35-36 (paraphrase) · the Torah service in the synagogue (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: was lost, and is found
neighbors.text: Today forty men who had signed themselves out came back, and the Guru tore up the paper. Jesus told of a son who took his share and left. When he came home, his father saw him a long way off, ran to him, and threw a feast: "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found."
neighbors.difference: In the parable, the son comes home alive and the father's welcome comes first, before any proof. At Muktsar, the forty proved their return with their lives, and the Guru's blessing came at the end.
neighbors.shared: the door you walked out of can still be the door back in.

neighbors.heading: despair not
neighbors.text: Today forty men who had written themselves out came back, and the paper was torn. The Qur'an speaks to everyone who has wandered: "Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins." A hadith says God is gladder at a servant's return than a traveler who finds his lost camel, with all his food and water, in the desert.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, turning back, tawba, is between a person and God, open until the last breath, with no one else needed. At Muktsar, the return came in the Guru's presence, and the sangat still remembers it in the Ardas.
neighbors.shared: nobody is too far gone to turn around and come home.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 39:53 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, hadith of the lost camel (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: dust to dust
neighbors.text: Today a family let ashes go into the Sutlej, and still heard the wedding song. On Ash Wednesday, as ashes touch their foreheads, Catholics may hear words from Genesis: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." At a funeral Mass, the Church grieves, and prays in hope that the one who died will rise with Christ.
neighbors.difference: The Church allows cremation but asks that ashes be kept in a sacred place, like a cemetery, not scattered, in hope of the body's resurrection. The Sikh code invites ashes into any flowing water and discourages monuments.
neighbors.shared: grief and hope can stand side by side at a goodbye.
neighbors.sources: Genesis 3:19 (Douay-Rheims) · Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Ad resurgendum cum Christo (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: all things pass
neighbors.text: Today a family let ashes go into the river, and the current took them at once. When the Buddha died, the texts say, his body was cremated and the relics shared among those who loved him. His last words, as one old translation has them: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!"
neighbors.difference: Buddhists built stupas over the Buddha's relics, places to visit and remember. The Sikh code discourages monuments over ashes, and the Kirtan Sohila sees death as a soul going home to God.
neighbors.shared: letting go gently is one more way of loving.

neighbors.heading: a tent open on all sides
neighbors.text: Today the Harmandir's doors opened on all four sides, so nobody came in by a back way. The rabbis told the same of Abraham. His tent, they said, had openings on every side, so a traveler from any direction could walk straight in. Genesis shows him sitting at the tent door in the heat, then running to welcome three strangers.
neighbors.difference: Abraham's tent is a story of one household welcoming guests. The Harmandir's doors are read as a teaching about society: people of all four classes of Guru Arjan's day equally welcome in one house of worship.
neighbors.shared: a good door faces whoever is coming.

neighbors.heading: unscrew the doors
neighbors.text: Today a building preached without a word: doors on every side, and a step down to come in. Walt Whitman wanted a poem built the same way, open to every kind of person. In Song of Myself he cries: "Unscrew the locks from the doors! / Unscrew the doors themselves from their jambs!" Everyone, he insists, belongs in the song.
neighbors.difference: Whitman's open doors belong to a poet: a self wide enough to hold everyone, with no house of worship. The Harmandir's doors are marble and gold around the Guru's word, and they welcome you in to bow.
neighbors.shared: you can tell who's welcome by how the doors are built.
neighbors.sources: Walt Whitman, Song of Myself, section 24 (Leaves of Grass)

neighbors.heading: the better way
neighbors.text: Today two men argued over tea about a calendar, and a teenager kept filling both cups. The Qur'an asks for that tone: "Call unto the way of thy Lord with wisdom and fair exhortation, and reason with them in the better way." Muslim scholars built schools of law that differ on many questions, and their followers still pray side by side.
neighbors.difference: In Islam, the schools of law are accepted as different paths of careful reasoning, each with its own rulings. The Sikh panth keeps one shared code, the Rehat Maryada, and leaves room inside it for questions still open.
neighbors.shared: you can disagree and still pour the other person's tea.

neighbors.heading: say their side first
neighbors.text: Today the Sikh code admitted a question was open, and kept the book whole. Hindu thinkers built a habit for open questions: the purvapaksha, the other side's view, laid out fully and fairly before the answer comes. Commentators such as Shankara wrote whole passages in an opponent's voice. The schools of Hindu thought argued hard, and kept honoring the same Vedas.
neighbors.difference: In Hindu thought, many schools stand side by side with no single code or authority over them all. Sikhs keep one Granth and one shared code, and hold their open questions inside that frame.
neighbors.shared: hear the other side well enough to say it back.
neighbors.sources: the purvapaksha method, e.g. Shankara's commentary on the Brahma Sutras (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the three jewels
neighbors.text: Today the panth looked like a banyan: many sangats, one Guru. Buddhism grew wide too, into many schools: Theravada in Sri Lanka and Thailand, Zen in Japan, Tibetan lineages in the Himalayas. Robes, chants and languages differ. Yet across them, Buddhists take refuge in the same three jewels: the Buddha, the Dhamma, his teaching, and the Sangha, the community.
neighbors.difference: Buddhist schools keep different collections of scripture, in Pali, Chinese and Tibetan. Sikh streams bow to one and the same book, the Guru Granth Sahib.
neighbors.shared: one root can hold up a very wide tree.

neighbors.heading: many members, one body
neighbors.text: Today a faith with many streams turned out to be a banyan, wide because it's alive. Paul answered the same worry in Corinth: "Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit." And: "For as the body is one, and hath many members... so also is Christ." The eye, he says, can't tell the hand, I have no need of you.
neighbors.difference: For Paul, the many gifts are held together in one body, Christ, by the Spirit. In Sikh teaching, the many sangats are held together by one Guru, the Granth, and one light in everyone.
neighbors.shared: being different doesn't stop us from belonging to each other.

neighbors.heading: what's up to you
neighbors.text: Today a farmer couldn't make it rain, and still got up to plow. Epictetus, a Stoic teacher who had been a slave, began his handbook right there: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Our choices and efforts are ours; weather, bodies and other people are not. Do your part fully, he taught, and meet the rest calmly.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus saw the world ordered by nature and reason, and found calm in his own judgments. Sikh teaching names the order hukam, the will of the One God, and walks in it by remembering the Name.
neighbors.shared: do your part fully, and let the sky be the sky.

neighbors.heading: God works in you
neighbors.text: Today a farmer plowed under a sky she couldn't control: effort inside the order, not against it. Paul tells the Philippians to "work out your salvation" with fear and trembling, then adds: "For it is God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish, according to his good will." The Church teaches that God lets people truly share in his plan.
neighbors.difference: Catholic teaching speaks of providence and grace working with free will, and of salvation through Christ. Sikh teaching speaks of the hukam, the order of the One, and of walking in it through the Name.
neighbors.shared: your effort and God's order aren't rivals; they work together.
neighbors.sources: Philippians 2:12-13 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 306-307 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the self, your friend
neighbors.text: Today the Gurus spoke to the restless mind as a friend: you are the form of the light. The Bhagavad Gita says something close. Krishna tells Arjuna to lift the self by the self, and not let it sink: the self is its own friend, and its own enemy. For one who has mastered it, the mind is a friend; for one who hasn't, it acts like a foe.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the mind is trained through meditation and discipline, turned toward the Self within. The Gurus give the mind the shabad, the Word, and the Name to hold.
neighbors.shared: the voice in your head can become a friend.

neighbors.heading: with both your hearts
neighbors.text: Today the Gurus didn't throw the restless mind out; they gave it work. The rabbis read the Shema closely: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart." The Hebrew word for heart has a doubled letter, and the Mishnah reads it: love God with both inclinations, the good one and the evil one. Even the urge that pulls you around can be put to holy use.
neighbors.difference: Jewish teaching names two inclinations inside a person and channels both through the commandments. The Gurus speak of one mind, man, that can wander or rest, and give it the Word to hold.
neighbors.shared: even your restless side can be turned toward good.

neighbors.heading: that he may have to give
neighbors.text: Today money wasn't the enemy: earn with honest hands, then open them. Paul says nearly the same in one sentence: "Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth." Work honestly, then give. The earning has a purpose beyond the earner.
neighbors.difference: Paul sets no share for giving; some Christians tithe a tenth, others give as they're able. Sikh tradition names dasvandh, a tenth, and pairs it with the open kitchen of the langar.
neighbors.shared: honest work gives your hands something to share.

neighbors.heading: from his own hands
neighbors.text: Today the salok honored the one who earns by work and gives from their hand. The Prophet Muhammad praised the same pair. In a hadith, he says no one eats better food than what they earn with their own hands, and that the prophet David ate from his own labor. Then comes zakat: a set share of wealth, given each year to those in need.
neighbors.difference: Zakat is a required pillar of Islam, with set amounts and set recipients. Dasvandh, the Sikh tenth, is a tradition given to the community and those in need, beside the everyday sharing called vand chhakna.
neighbors.shared: money earned honestly is meant to move toward someone in need.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith on eating from one's own labor (paraphrase) · Qur'an 9:60 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: comforted to comfort
neighbors.text: Today Farid climbed high and saw the same fire in every house. Paul tells the Corinthians that God comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort others in theirs. The Church teaches that suffering, joined to Christ's cross, doesn't have to be wasted, and calls everyone to stay close to those who suffer.
neighbors.difference: For Catholics, suffering offered with Christ's can share in his saving work. In the Gurus' line, pain is a bitter medicine that wakes a person to remember God.
neighbors.shared: nobody should be left alone with their fire.
neighbors.sources: 2 Corinthians 1:3-4 (paraphrase) · John Paul II, Salvifici Doloris (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the mustard seed
neighbors.text: Today Farid climbed high and saw a fire burning in every house. Buddhists tell of Kisa Gotami, who carried her dead child to the Buddha. Bring me a mustard seed, he said, from a house where no one has died. She knocked on door after door. Every house had lost someone. She came back without a seed, and with understanding.
neighbors.difference: The Buddha's first teaching names suffering, its cause in craving, and a path to its end. The Gurus call pain a medicine that wakes a person to remember God.
neighbors.shared: your pain is real, and you aren't the only one carrying it.
neighbors.sources: the story of Kisa Gotami, Therigatha and Dhammapada commentaries (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: slow to anger
neighbors.text: Today the Gurus named anger a thief that burns its own hand first. Proverbs says: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." The rabbis add that anger makes the wise forget their wisdom, and say that even Moses, once angry, forgot a teaching.
neighbors.difference: Jewish teaching describes God as slow to anger and asks people to walk in God's ways. The Gurus name anger one of five thieves inside the body, and answer it with simran, remembering the Name.
neighbors.shared: a pause before the angry word is a kind of strength.

neighbors.heading: delay is the cure
neighbors.text: Today the Gurus asked for one breath before the angry word. The Stoic Seneca wrote a whole book on anger and landed in the same place: the greatest remedy for anger is delay. Let the first heat pass, he advised; anger cools while it waits. He saw what Farid saw too: anger wounds the one who carries it.
neighbors.difference: Seneca wanted anger gone almost entirely, even against wrongdoing, with reason alone in charge. The Gurus allow a fierce stand against cruelty done to others, steered by compassion and the remembrance of God.
neighbors.shared: one breath can be the difference between a burn and a choice.

neighbors.heading: until ye come to the graves
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said the hunger of the hungry doesn't go away, however much they pile up. The Qur'an says it bluntly: "Rivalry in worldly increase distracteth you / Until ye come to the graves." A hadith adds: if a person had a valley of gold, they'd want a second, and nothing fills their mouth but dust.
neighbors.difference: Islam answers greed with zakat, a required yearly gift, and gratitude to God as the giver of everything. The Gurus name greed one of five inner thieves, and answer it with honest work, sharing and the Name.
neighbors.shared: enough is a small word that can set you free.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 102:1-2 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari, hadith of the valley of gold (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: fire and ghee
neighbors.text: Today greed was the thief whose finish line keeps sliding forward. Hindu texts give a picture: desire is never quenched by getting what it wants; it grows like a fire fed with ghee. The Mahabharata tells of King Yayati, who borrowed his son's youth for more years of pleasure, and found the hunger still there. The Gita calls greed a gate to ruin.
neighbors.difference: Some Hindu paths answer desire with renunciation, even leaving home for an ascetic life. The Gurus keep a person at home and at work, and answer greed with honest earning, sharing and the Name.
neighbors.shared: more doesn't fill the hunger; enough does.
neighbors.sources: Manusmriti 2.94 (paraphrase) · Mahabharata, Adi Parva, the story of Yayati (paraphrase) · Bhagavad Gita 16:21 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a flower without scent
neighbors.text: Today a family prayed before a long drive, and then someone picked up the car keys. The Dhammapada has a picture for words with no deeds behind them: "Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly." The teaching is meant to be done, not only recited.
neighbors.difference: In Buddhism, practice centers on one's own effort and mindful conduct, without prayer to a creator God. The Sikh line braids prayer to God, honest work and sharing into one life.
neighbors.shared: good words come alive when your hands follow them.

neighbors.heading: be ye warmed and filled
neighbors.text: Today a prayer for a hungry neighbor ended at the stove. The letter of James paints the opposite: "If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit?"
neighbors.difference: James ties deeds to faith in Christ: faith without works, he says, is dead. The Sikh line ties them to remembering the Name: prayer first, so the work has a source, then work, so the prayer goes somewhere.
neighbors.shared: a prayer for the hungry ends with a full plate.

neighbors.heading: the stranger's right
neighbors.text: Today the door stayed open, and the guest got the good cup. The philosopher Immanuel Kant argued that hospitality isn't only kindness; it's a right. A stranger who arrives in another land, he wrote, has the right not to be treated as an enemy, because we all share the surface of the same earth.
neighbors.difference: Kant's hospitality is a minimum owed to any stranger, grounded in reason and a shared planet. Sikh welcome sets out a seat and a meal, because God is within every guest.
neighbors.shared: whoever knocks is welcome before you know who they are.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace, Third Definitive Article (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: received as Christ
neighbors.text: Today a guest arrived and the house rearranged itself around them. Saint Benedict wrote it into his Rule for monks: let every guest who comes be received as Christ, for he will say, I was a stranger and you took me in. The Rule even asks the abbot and the community to wash the guests' feet.
neighbors.difference: For Benedict, the guest is welcomed as Christ himself, arriving unrecognized. In Sikh teaching, the guest is welcomed because God is within everyone, and no one stands outside the household.
neighbors.shared: every guest at the door deserves the good cup.
neighbors.sources: Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 53 (paraphrase) · Matthew 25:35 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: how the good walk
neighbors.text: Today a way of life was worn in like a path across a lawn, then written down. Hindus call the right way dharma, and Manu's code names where to find it: the Veda, the remembered teachings, the conduct of good people, and what satisfies one's own conscience. Good people walking the way are part of the map.
neighbors.difference: Hindu dharma is spread across many texts and teachers, and shaped by one's stage of life and duties. The Sikh Rehat Maryada is one written code meant for the whole panth.
neighbors.shared: a good way is made by the people who walk it every day.

neighbors.heading: the way to walk
neighbors.text: Today a code turned out to be a path, worn in by people walking it a day at a time. Jews call their way of life halakha, which tradition hears as the walking, the way one goes. Jethro tells Moses to teach the people God's laws, "and shalt show them the way wherein they must walk, and the work that they must do."
neighbors.difference: Halakha grows through generations of rabbinic debate and rulings, and communities follow different authorities. The Sikh Rehat Maryada is one written code meant for the whole panth.
neighbors.shared: faith becomes a path when you take it one step at a time.
